To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

people with stronger tendencies to link effort with outcomes complicate what should be easy choices by: (a). distorting their evaluations of the alternatives; (b) distoring information recalled about the options; (c) distorting interpretations and evaluations of information about the options; and (d) conducting a superfluous information search and spending more time than needed to finalize their choice.

the work ethic heuristic (i.e., the tendency to link effort and positive outcomes) causes individuals to distort their evaluations and information search and recall, thereby complicating what should have been easy decisions.

individuals who believe that effort is linked to positive outcomes (e. g., those subscribing to Protestant work ethic beliefs) tend to distort their preferences in a manner that complicates decisions, and that this tendency is due to the belief that effort is linked with positive outcomes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of effort in decision making.
the way individuals process information and make decisions when the outcome of a decision is uncertain.
the role of the work ethic in decision making.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Protestant Work Ethic heuristic, which is the tendency of people to link effort with desirable outcomes, can complicate decision-making by distorting evaluations of decision alternatives, information recalled and interpreted about these alternatives, and the time spent in decision making.

individuals who subscribe to Protestant work ethic (PWE) are shown to distort evaluations of alternatives, distort information recalled about the alternative, distort interpretation of information about the alternative and spend more time on what should have an easy decision.

the Protestant Work Ethic (PWE) is an ideology that is deeply rooted in the Western culture and that it is a powerful heuristic that can be activated by different cues and that it can have a profound impact on the way we think about effort and outcomes, and on the decisions we make.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
individuals with a strong tendency to link effort and positive outcomes are prone to distort their decisions and to engage in unnecessary decisional effort.
individuals with a strong Protestant Work Ethic are likely to experience a conflict-increasing bias in their choices.
people who subscribe to the Protestant Work Ethic (PWE) have a tendency to overestimate the difficulty and effort involved in making a choice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the tendency to believe that effort leads to positive outcomes (e. g., the Protestant Work Ethic, PWE) can have negative consequences on decision making.
people with a stronger tendency of linking effort with positive outcomes tend to overcomplicate decisions.
the work ethic heuristic can lead people to complicate their lives by distorting information in a way that makes it more difficult to choose between alternatives.
